title: From Hallucination to Reliability: Generative Modeling and the Structure of Scientific Inference
extended_summary:
This paper addresses a conceptual problem in the use of generative AI for scientific inference: how to understand and manage hallucination without rejecting these models as epistemically unreliable. The author argues that common, data-centric definitions of hallucination are too restrictive because they treat any deviation from the training data as an error, even when such deviation may reflect genuine scientific discovery.

The paper proposes a phenomenon-centric account of hallucination, defining it as a non-strategic misrepresentation of the target phenomenon produced by the model itself rather than inherited from the training data. Using this lens, the paper analyzes how scientific workflows can discipline generative models through theory-guided training and confidence-based error screening. Two case studies are examined: AlphaFold 3 in protein structure prediction and GenCast in weather forecasting. In both cases, theoretical constraints are built into training and uncertainty estimates are used to flag unreliable outputs.

The paper does not study human participants, classrooms, or K-12 learners. Instead, it is a theoretical/philosophical paper about scientific AI systems and the epistemic conditions under which their outputs can support reliable inference. Its main conclusion is that hallucination need not undermine the use of generative AI in science when models are embedded in mature, theory-rich workflows that make errors detectable and manageable.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/philosophical paper with case illustrations, not an empirical K-12 study, RCT, QED, or meta-analysis. It does not provide a clear evaluative methodology for student outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: No direct educational intervention or student outcome is evaluated, so there is no measurable K-12 impact estimate. The paper is relevant to reliability concerns, but it does not demonstrate impact in practice.

interventions.use_case: Conceptual analysis of generative AI used for scientific inference, focusing on AlphaFold 3 protein structure prediction and GenCast weather forecasting as examples of reliability, hallucination, and error screening workflows.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is primarily a theoretical/reliability analysis rather than an intervention study. It argues that generative scientific AI can support reliable inference when embedded in theory-guided training and confidence-based screening, but also emphasizes that hallucinations are inevitable and can mislead when not properly managed. No experimental effect size is reported because the paper does not present a K-12 outcome evaluation.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of reliability, hallucination, and inferential workflows in scientific AI (AlphaFold 3, GenCast)
